title: The Missionaries of Charity (1950)
hookLine: the sisters in white and blue saris, begun by Teresa of Calcutta, who care for the dying

cards: A long room in Kolkata, beside a Hindu temple. Rows of low beds, each holding someone found on the street, too sick to walk.
A sister in a white sari with blue stripes kneels at one of them with a basin of water, washing a man's feet. He may not live through the week, and she knows it. She isn't there to cure him.
She's there so that he doesn't die alone, unwashed, unnamed. The house is called Nirmal Hriday. The sisters are the Missionaries of Charity.

teach.b: The order was begun by the woman Catholics now call Saint Teresa of Calcutta, Mother Teresa, a teacher who left her convent school to live among the city's poorest people. Start with the promise.

Like other sisters, they make vows of poverty, chastity and obedience, and their rule adds one more: wholehearted and free service to the poorest of the poor. Free means no payment, ever. Then the thirst.

In their chapels, beside the crucifix, the sisters put two words from the cross in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "I thirst." They hear in them Jesus thirsting for love, and they see him in the person on the bed.

Then the work, which grew far beyond Kolkata: homes for the dying, for abandoned children, for people with leprosy or AIDS, soup kitchens in big Western cities. There are brothers and priests in the same family now too.
The work is plain: washing, feeding, sitting, holding a hand. And the questions.
Not everyone has praised it. Some critics, including doctors who visited, questioned the standard of medical care in the homes.
Supporters answer that the homes were meant for comfort and presence at the end, not hospital treatment.

Both are part of the honest story. Today's line comes from a British journalist who filmed the sisters and called his book Something Beautiful for God, after a phrase tradition links with Mother Teresa.
Not something impressive. Something beautiful, like a clean bed and a held hand.

how: Missionaries of Charity sisters, in their white saris with blue borders, run homes for the dying, the abandoned and the sick in many countries, and volunteers of any faith or none can often come to help with the daily washing, feeding and cleaning.

games.q: you're a sister in Kolkata. a man found on the street is dying, and no treatment will save him. what do you do?
o: send him to a hospital that will turn him away.
wash him, feed him and stay with him.
move on to someone who can be cured.
games.why: the sisters wash, feed and sit with the dying, so no one dies alone and unnamed.

practice: Hold in mind someone who is dying or very ill: a grandparent, a friend in a hospice, a stranger in a hospital you passed. Picture their room and someone sitting with them, and ask, gently, whether that someone could ever be you.
If you pray, pray for them and for all who care for the dying; if not, simply hold them in mind.
